prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, The, Not

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the poem's fragmented, elegiac style and original imagery while refining its rhythm and diction:

---

When the bed lies empty, we draw the shades against the light—light akin to memory, the long light of waiting, an impatience simmering in its glow. The here of the now, and the glow that days cast upon the room, absent the body yet steeped in its trace. So we speak of vacancy and abjection, set against the *was*, against a philosophy of *once* and *then no more*. A not-being, held in opposition. A child once grew here—etched as lines upon a wall, growing without knowledge of what would one day cease to be. A gnawing takes root. It grew, and then it was. Protection curls inward. Motionless.

I envy her, in her room—hers, with paint and dolls and handprints. Great green light glowing beneath blankets, a hand that nurtures the heart of the mouth, murmurs into it, loves the heart entire. A heart beating within another—blood blushing—God, the beating, illumined, doing only what it must.

---

I preserved the original's deliberate ambiguity, sentence fragments, and emotional cadence, while smoothing transitions (e.g., "growing without knowing what would one day not be" → "growing without knowledge of what would one day cease to be") and tightening a few phrases for clarity and musicality. Let me know if you'd like a version that leans even more toward the experimental/broken syntax of the original, or one that's more conventionally lyrical.
outputs.L2: When the bed sits vacant, we draw the curtains to shut out light—light that echoes recollection, a lingering brightness of anticipation, restlessness humming beneath its glow. The present moment and the glow days cast upon the room, absent of the body yet still carrying its lingering scent. So we name it: emptiness and desolation, standing against what has passed, against any notion of existing once and then ceasing to exist. Opposition to nonexistence itself. A child once flourished within these walls. Marked in pencil strokes along the wall. Growing, unaware that growth would someday halt. An ache expands. Something that flourished and then simply was. Shelter now folded inward. Still and unmoving. I find myself envying her, in her own room. Hers, filled with paint smears and dolls and palm prints pressed into surfaces. A rich green light glowing beneath covers, a hand tending to the core of a small mouth, murmuring softly against it, cherishing that heart. A heart pulsing inside another body—blood rushing warm with color—God, that pulse, illuminated, simply continuing its work.
outputs.L3:
I pull the shades down in the empty room, though there is no one left to protect from morning. The light that seeps through anyway is the kind that keeps memory alive against my will—a persistent, golden intrusion that makes me wait, though I no longer know what I am waiting for. It arrives at the same hour it always did, indifferent to what the room has become, and I find myself resenting its punctuality, its refusal to acknowledge that everything has changed. I stand there in the half-dark I've manufactured, impatient with a light that insists on shining as if nothing has happened here, as if this were still an ordinary room in an ordinary house.

But the room does not let go so easily. Even shaded, even stilled, it holds onto something—a glow that seems to seep from the walls themselves, and beneath it, a smell that has not yet surrendered to time. It is the scent of days once filled, of a body that moved through this space with such constancy that the air itself seemed to memorize it. Now that body is gone, and yet the room breathes as if it might return, as if the absence were only temporary, a pause rather than an ending.

I have come to resist the finality that others seem so ready to accept. There is a violence in the phrase *once and then not*—as though a life could be folded into two clean halves, severed by a single moment, and everything before rendered obsolete by everything after. I will not grant the room that logic. To call this space empty is to admit a kind of surrender I am not yet prepared to make. Vacancy, I have decided, is not the same as absence—it can be a stance, a refusal, a way of holding open what the world would rather have closed.

Along the wall, faint pencil lines still mark where a child once stood, straightening on tiptoe to see how much taller they'd grown since the last time someone measured. Each mark is a small monument to becoming, to the specific miracle of a body lengthening year by year, inch by inch, until it filled a doorway, a bed, a life. Now those lines measure nothing but stillness. The child who once could not stop moving, could not stop growing into the world, has folded into something small and curled, motionless in a way that feels less like rest and more like protection—a body curved inward as if to shield itself from what has already happened, or perhaps to shield the room from having to witness it.

And so I find myself, absurdly, envying another child entirely—one who lives somewhere else, in a room bursting with color: paint on the walls in uneven, joyful streaks, dolls arranged in the particular chaos only a child could design, small handprints pressed into the plaster like proof of a life still being written. That child's room hums with a different kind of light, one that isn't asking to be blocked out. Somewhere, a heart beats quietly beneath a chest that expects to grow and grow, uninterrupted, into all the years still owed to it. I envy that unbroken rhythm, that heartbeat allowed to simply continue, nurturing itself forward without having to justify its own persistence. I envy the world that lets it.
outputs.L4:
# Untitled

The room stays exactly as it was left. This is the first cruelty—that nothing rearranges itself in sympathy, that the walls do not know how to grieve. The window still lets in light, though someone has drawn the curtain halfway, as if light itself needed rationing now, needed permission to enter a space that no longer holds what it once held.

There is a doorframe with pencil marks. Small dates. Small heights. A hand that is no longer growing pressed against wood that will now outlast it, testimony to a body's ascension measured in inches, in years, stopped now mid-sentence, mid-inch, mid-becoming. The marks do not know they are the last marks. They simply are, the way small marks are, thin evidence of accumulation, of someone standing very straight, very proud, being measured, being seen, being loved enough to be recorded.

The plants by the window have not been told. They continue their slow work of turning toward light, indifferent to the arithmetic of loss, and this indifference feels almost like an accusation. How dare the green things continue. How dare the light continue to fall in its patterns across the floor, marking hours that no longer need marking, that no longer accumulate toward anything.

*Was.* The word sits strange in the mouth, a stone that shouldn't be swallowed but is. *Was* implies a symmetry with *is*, some kind of grammatical justice, but there is no *is* to balance it, only the sprawling, formless territory of *not-being*—which is not the same as absence, not the same as simply gone, but something stranger: the persistent shape of a presence that has been subtracted, leaving behind its silhouette the way light leaves a shadow on a wall that has faded in the sun, a ghost-rectangle where a picture frame once hung.

Envy arrives, unbidden, unwanted, ashamed of itself. Envy for the neighbors' laughter through the wall, for the mother pushing a stroller who does not know—cannot know—the particular alchemy that transforms an ordinary Tuesday into an anniversary of unbearable weight. Envy for continuance itself, for the audacity of other lives simply proceeding, as if proceeding were not itself a kind of violence against the one who cannot.

And beneath the envy, something that might be grief but wears grief's clothing loosely, uncertain of its own name. Because grief implies a shape, a process, a known arc that bends eventually toward acceptance. But this—this is closer to a physical fact. This is closer to the pulse in the wrist that continues its stupid, faithful rhythm no matter what the mind commands it to feel, no matter how the mind might wish to cease alongside what has ceased.

The body does not know how to stop. This is its final betrayal and its final mercy, indistinguishable from one another. Lungs fill. Blood moves. The stubborn animal persistence of flesh continues its work regardless of the absence it must now carry, regardless of the room down the hall that stays exactly as it was left, holding its light-blocked window, its pencil marks, its small and terrible evidence of a life that was, that is no longer, that leaves in its wake this strange arithmetic: the more absent the presence, the more aware the body becomes of its own relentless, beating, unwanted continuation.

This is the cruelty of survival. This is the cruelty of walls that do not grieve, of plants that do not know, of pencil marks that stay precisely where they were drawn, refusing to rise any higher, refusing to mark another year, another inch, another proof of becoming—while somewhere beneath the ribs, something keeps insisting on tomorrow.
outputs.L5:
# When The Not

There is a peculiar power in incomplete words, in fragments that ask us to fill in the silence between them. *When. The. Not.* Three words, none of them nouns, none of them verbs—only markers, hinges on which larger thoughts might turn.

**When** speaks to time, to the moment before something happens and the moment after. It is the word of anticipation and memory, of "when I was young" and "when it finally comes." We live suspended between two whens: the one behind us, already fixed and unchangeable, and the one ahead, still soft with possibility.

**The** is different. It is the word of specificity, of pointing. Not *a* moment, but *the* moment. Not *a* person, but *the* person. It transforms the abstract into the particular, drawing a circle around one thing among many and saying: this one matters. Language without "the" would drift, unanchored, never quite arriving anywhere.

**Not** is the quiet rebel of language—the word of refusal, of boundary, of what could have been but isn't. It defines by exclusion. To say what something is *not* is often the fastest way to understand what it *is*. Negation carves shape out of formlessness.

Together, these three words resist forming a sentence. They ask instead to be inhabited, turned over, sat with. *When* is the not-yet and the no-longer. *The* is the insistence that something specific is happening. *Not* is the space where meaning still waits to be decided.

Perhaps that is the lesson embedded in these three small words: that meaning is rarely found in the answer, but in the tension of the asking—in the moment *when* we are still deciding what *the* thing is, and what it is *not*.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about grief and an empty child's room, using fragmented syntax and repetition.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Room**

The door. The door still. The door still closes the way it always—

Small shoes by the door. Two of them. Facing out like he might.
Facing out like he might just.

*Not yet. Not yet. Not yet.*

The bed made. Who made the bed. I made the bed. I make the bed
every morning I make the bed every morning the bed does not
need making no one has slept no one has slept in—

*Don't touch the pillow. Don't touch. Don't.*

Dust on the windowsill collecting light collecting the shape of afternoons
he is not walking through. A room can hold a shape. A room
can hold the exact temperature of a Tuesday. This Tuesday. Every
Tuesday now is this Tuesday.

The wallpaper: little boats. Little boats going nowhere, going
nowhere so patiently. Going nowhere with such small blue sails.

*I painted his name on the door myself.*
*I painted his name.*
*His name is still on the door.*

Say it. Say the name. The name catches
in the throat like a door
that will not
close. That will not.

Toys arranged not by him. By me. By me arranging
what he arranged differently. He would not
have lined them up. He would have—

*left them anywhere. Anywhere at all. Anywhere.*

The window. Someone left the window. I did not
leave the window. Yet the curtain moves
the way it moved when he

when he

when.

Grief is a room you keep. Grief is a room
you keep exactly as it was exactly
as it was exactly as it was
until *exactly* becomes a kind of prayer,
a kind of door,
a kind of small shoe
facing out,
still facing out,
still waiting for a foot
that fit it once,
that fit it
once.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal, stream-of-consciousness piece exploring loss, absence, and the lingering presence of a child who is gone.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the House Keeps

The shoes by the door still face outward, ready for feet that would run before walking was even mastered, and I have stopped moving them because moving them would mean admitting the door remembers better than I do—

there is a height chart in pencil on the frame of the kitchen doorway, marks like a musical staff with no notes left to play, and some mornings I catch the door breathing in the old way, expanding to the size of a child not yet a child, still folded into next Tuesday, into a birthday that arrives like a tide that forgot the moon—

the milk goes bad in the same rhythm it always did, seven days, though the mouth that drank it is elsewhere, is everywhere, is the specific nowhere that swallows the specific somewhere a body used to occupy—

I fold the small shirts into the drawer and they refold themselves into wings, I am not surprised, grief makes seamstresses of us all, cutting fabric into shapes that almost fit the absence, almost—

there is a sound the swing set makes when the wind moves through it, metal singing a song with the child's laugh removed but the shape of the laugh still hollowed into the note, like a bell that keeps the shape of the moment after ringing—

the calendar refuses April, folds it into thirds like a letter never sent, and I keep receiving April anyway, it comes wearing the wrong face, it comes asking for cereal, for socks, for the specific blue that only existed in one pair of eyes—

I talk to the dent in the couch cushion. It has learned to hold its shape without the weight. This is either devotion or the physics of foam remembering, I no longer distinguish—

sometimes the absence sits at the table and reaches for the salt and I pass it because what else do you do when the air asks politely, what else do you do when your hands still know the motion better than your mind knows the math—

the photographs have started dreaming without me, I find them rearranged, the child now standing where the dog once stood, now sitting where I once sat, the pixels renegotiating the terms of what happened, what could have happened, what happens still in the tense that grief invented—the was-still-is—

there is a room. I do not enter the room. The room enters me instead, nightly, carrying its small furniture into my chest, arranging and rearranging, an interior decorator with no client, no deadline, all the time already spent—

the child is not gone. The child is the space between one word and the next, is the pause where I used to say *be careful* and now say nothing, the sentence still built, still standing, just missing its exclamation point, its listener, its living proof—

I keep setting one extra plate. It's not madness. It's mathematics. Love doesn't know how to subtract. Love only knows how to keep counting the ones who counted, keeps the tally running even when the tally-taker is the only one left in the room, keeps saying *this many, this many, this many were loved, this many are loved still*—

and the house holds its breath in the shape of a child, and I hold my breath in the shape of the house, and somewhere in that doubled inhale, that borrowed lung, we go on, we go on, we go on being the place where someone almost still lives.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic meditation on emptiness and memory, focusing on light, shadows, and a bedroom once occupied by a child.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Room That Held You

The light still finds the window at four o'clock,
same slant, same gold, same patient arithmetic
of hours—it does not know you've gone.
It pools upon the floor where blocks once stood,
where dinosaurs marched armies through the dust,
and finding nothing there to cast a shadow,
makes none. This is what absence looks like:
not darkness, but light with nothing to interrupt it.

The walls remember height in pencil marks,
a ladder climbing toward a ceiling
you were always, always reaching for.
Someone should erase them. No one does.
They stand like small confessions of the years,
evidence that time was once a thing
that happened visibly, in inches, in a doorframe.

I come here sometimes when the house is quiet
and sit inside the shape you left in air—
that particular emptiness only a child's leaving
can carve, distinct from other kinds of gone.
The bed is made. The bed is always made now,
smooth as a held breath, smooth as forgetting
would be if forgetting were a mercy
and not this—this keeping, this small museum
of a person still becoming, paused.

Shadows move differently in rooms like this.
They don't fall so much as settle, as if tired
of pretending there's a reason to be cast
by anything but light itself, that indifferent architect
who builds the same cathedral every afternoon
and never asks who's there to see it rise.

I do not dust the shelf of small good books.
I do not touch the closet's careful hangers,
their emptiness a kind of punctuation
at the end of sentences I can't finish.
This is not a shrine. I don't believe in shrines.
It's just a room. It's just the light, arriving
faithfully, finding no one, and staying anyway—
the way that memory does, the way that love,
having nowhere left to put itself,
becomes a kind of weather in a house,
becomes the quality of afternoon
in every room that used to hold a child
and now holds only this: the gold, the dust,
the patient unrelenting shine of what remains
when everything that mattered has moved on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, abstract text about mourning that plays with grammar and negation ("not-being," "was," "then not") to express absence.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains When Absence Speaks

There was. That is the whole grammar of it—*there was*, past tense, a country
you can never emigrate back to.

He was here. Not "he is here, elsewhere." Not "he continues, unseen."
*Was.* The verb closes like a door closes, not with violence
but with the terrible ordinariness of doors.

I keep almost-summoning the present tense.
My mouth begins *he is*— and then the not arrives,
soft-footed, patient, correcting me
the way a parent corrects a child's grammar,
except the parent is silence
and the child is every sentence I try to build him a house in.

Not-being is not nothing.
Nothing would be easier—nothing doesn't ache,
doesn't sit in his chair with the specific weight of an absence
shaped exactly like him.
This is not-being: being's shadow, cast backward,
falling through the same window
at the same hour
the light finds empty.

Then not.
Between *then* and *not* is where I live now—
that thin hyphen, that catch in the throat of time,
the seam where a life
was sewn shut.

I say *was* and the word is a small grave
I dig with my tongue each time I speak of him,
each was another handful of earth,
gentle, necessary, unbearable.

And yet—
grammar insists on a future.
*Will* keeps arriving uninvited,
some clause of mine still reaching forward
into a sentence he is not in,
and I let it, I let the will,
because to stop reaching
would be its own kind of *not*,
and I have had enough of nots
to last the grammar of a life.

So: he was.
So: I am.
So: between these verbs,
a whole ungrammatical love
persists—
not present, not past,
but conjugated in the aching tense
of everything that keeps almost-happening
in the shape where he isn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a highly figurative, punctuation-experimental poem about envy, love, and the ache of an empty room after a child’s death.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Room Keeps Its Own Weather

The door—still—a mouth that forgot its last word.
Sunlight comes in like a guest who wasn't told,
paces the floorboards, finds the small shoes (still there!
still waiting for feet that have gone to be weather
themselves) & doesn't know what to do with its hands.

I am jealous—god forgive me—of the mothers
whose grief is only *imagined*, a rehearsal
they get to walk home from. I covet
the ordinary Tuesday, its dumb mercy.
I covet you, stranger-with-a-living-child,
the way a burnt field covets rain
it can no longer use.

Love, they say, is a room you furnish
together—but what do you call the room
after? A museum. A wound with good lighting.
A held breath that forgot how to exhale
& so became the house's only weather:
the curtains move (there is no wind)
the closet holds its shape (there is no boy)

& envy—little green animal—
gnaws at the doorframe where his height
was marked in pencil, dates like rungs
on a ladder that led nowhere, or everywhere,
or just to this: a bed still made,
a nightlight no one has the courage
to unplug——because darkness, now,
would be one more small permission
we are not ready to give.

I loved him the way you love weather—
without asking, without proof,
a fact bigger than the sky that held it.
Now the sky is just a sky.
The room is just a room.
And I am just a woman standing
in a doorway, envying
everyone whose worst day
is still ahead of them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
